MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Happy to help. Here's everything in order.

**What "lippage" means**

Lippage is when one tile edge sits slightly higher than the tile next to it, so you get a small "lip" where they meet. You can feel it with bare feet or a sock, and it catches the light so it looks uneven. Longer tiles like your 30 × 60 cm ones are more prone to it, because they often have a very slight bow along their length. Two things help a lot:
- **Tile levelling clips**, which are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.
- **A brick-bond offset of no more than a third** of the tile length (about 20 cm). A 50% offset puts the high middle of one tile next to the low ends of its neighbour, which makes lippage worse.

**Grout colour for pale grey porcelain**

Go for a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**, or something like "pewter" or "steel grey." Floor grout darkens with dirt over time, so a slightly darker colour hides that, while still looking intentional against the pale tile. Avoid white or very light grey on a floor. A **stain-resistant or epoxy-modified grout**, or sealing a standard cement grout once it's cured, will keep it looking fresh much longer.

**Floor before or after the toilet?**

**Floor first.** Tiling the whole floor and then setting the toilet on top is much easier than cutting tiles around the pan's curved base, and it looks neater. It also means you won't have an untiled patch under the toilet if you ever replace it. Just check that the soil pipe connection still lines up once the floor is a centimetre or so higher.

**How many boxes to buy**

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, which rounds up to **27 tiles**
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, which rounds up to **4 boxes (32 tiles)**

**Buy 4 boxes.** That gives you 8 spare tiles, which is reassuring for a first project, and it's worth keeping a couple afterwards in case one ever cracks. Check that all the boxes have the same batch or shade number printed on them, as the colour can vary slightly between batches.

**Note to the neighbours**

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning for our bathroom floor, so there'll be some noise from about [time] for a few hours. We'll do our best to keep it as short as possible.
>
> Thank you so much for being patient with us, especially with the skip on the drive for the last couple of weeks. It's much appreciated, and it should all be wrapped up soon!
>
> [Your names, house number]

**Three tips for a first floor**

1. **Prepare the subfloor properly, because it matters more than the tiling.** The floor needs to be solid, flat, clean and dry. A timber floor that flexes needs to be overboarded with tile backer board or plywood first, or the tiles and grout will crack. Check flatness with a long straight edge and fix any dips before you start.
2. **Dry-lay the tiles and plan your layout before mixing any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out loose to see where the cuts will fall. Aim for cut pieces of at least half a tile at the edges, especially at the doorway, which is the most visible spot. Starting from a centre line usually gives balanced cuts on both sides.
3. **Work in small sections and check the adhesive coverage.** Mix adhesive in small batches so it doesn't skin over. Spread it with a notched trowel, and back-butter the tiles with a thin layer, which matters for 30 × 60 cm tiles. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check that the back is almost fully covered. Hollow spots are what lead to cracked tiles later.

One bonus tip: give yourself twice as long as the videos suggest, and don't walk on the floor until the adhesive has fully set. Good luck with it.
